title: Dreams — Philosophy × Psychology Timeline
content_html:
Dreams — Philosophy × Psychology Timeline

Start with Plato/Descartes for the epistemic puzzle
→ move to Freud/Jung for meaning
→ shift to activation–synthesis and continuity for naturalistic accounts
→ then predictive processing and lucid dreaming for contemporary mechanisms

  • Plato (4th c. BCE): Dreams problematize perception vs. knowledge; raise doubt about the distinction between appearance and reality (cf. Theaetetus). Dreams as a test case for what counts as knowledge.
  • Aristotle (4th c. BCE): Dreams as natural phenomena tied to sensation and imagination; not inherently supernatural.
  • Abrahamic traditions (5th–13th c.): Dreams variably treated as divine messages vs. illusions; scholastics integrate naturalistic accounts with theological meaning.
  • René Descartes (17th c.): The Dream Argument: if dreams feel indistinguishable from waking, sensory experience is not a secure foundation for certainty.
  • Sigmund Freud (1900): The Interpretation of Dreams: manifest vs. latent content; dream-work (condensation, displacement, symbolization).
  • C. G. Jung (20th c.): Dreams express archetypes of the collective unconscious; support individuation.

Neuroscience & Cognitive Science

  • Activation–Synthesis (1977): Brainstem activation during REM; cortex synthesizes a narrative: dreams as physiological, not necessarily meaningful.
  • Continuity & Neurocognitive Models (2000s–): Dreams reflect waking concerns and typical cognition; not ruled by special symbolism.
  • Threat Simulation (2000): Evolutionary function: rehearsal of dangers to improve preparedness.
  • Predictive Processing & Free-Energy* (2010s–): Dreams as offline generative modeling: the brain minimizes surprise by running simulations untethered from sensory input.
  • Lucid Dreaming & Two‑way Communication (2010s–2020s): Metacognition can return inside REM; studies show task‑related signals and simple dialogues with sleeping dreamers.
